{{Short description|Mathematical theory}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Twisted ''K''-theory}}
In mathematics, '''twisted K-theory''' (also called '''K-theory with local coefficients'''<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Donavan|first=Peter|last2=Karoubi|first2=Max|date=1970|title=Graded Brauer groups and $K$-theory with local coefficients|url=http://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1970__38__5_0/|journal=Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS|language=en|volume=38|pages=5–25}}</ref>) is a variation on [[K-theory]], a mathematical theory from the 1950s that spans [[algebraic topology]], [[abstract algebra]] and [[operator theory]].

More specifically, twisted K-theory with twist ''H'' is a particular variant of K-theory, in which the twist is given by an integral 3-dimensional [[cohomology class]]. It is special among the various twists that K-theory admits for two reasons.  First, it admits a geometric formulation. This was provided in two steps; the first one was done in 1970 (Publ. Math. de l'[[Institut des hautes études scientifiques|IHÉS]]) by Peter Donovan and Max Karoubi; the second one in 1988 by [[Jonathan Rosenberg (mathematician)|Jonathan Rosenberg]] in [https://web.archive.org/web/20060327202028/http://anziamj.austms.org.au/JAMSA/V47/Part3/Rosenberg.html Continuous-Trace Algebras from the Bundle Theoretic Point of View].

In physics, it has been conjectured to classify [[D-branes]], [[Ramond–Ramond field|Ramond-Ramond field strengths]] and in some cases even [[spinors]] in [[type II string theory]]. For more information on twisted K-theory in [[string theory]], see [[K-theory (physics)]].

In the broader context of K-theory, in each subject it has numerous [[isomorphic]] formulations and, in many cases, isomorphisms relating definitions in various subjects have been proven.  It also has numerous deformations, for example, in abstract algebra K-theory may be twisted by any integral cohomology class.

==Definition==
To motivate Rosenberg's geometric formulation of twisted K-theory, start from the [[Atiyah–Jänich theorem]], stating that

:<math>Fred(\mathcal H),</math>

the [[Fredholm operator]]s on [[Hilbert space]] <math>\mathcal H</math>, is a [[classifying space]] for ordinary, untwisted K-theory. This means that the K-theory of the space <math>M</math> consists of the [[homotopy class]]es of maps

:<math>[M\rightarrow Fred(\mathcal H)]</math>

from <math>M</math> to <math>Fred(\mathcal H).</math>

A slightly more complicated way of saying the same thing is as follows. Consider the [[trivial bundle]] of <math>Fred(\mathcal H)</math> over <math>M</math>, that is, the Cartesian product of <math>M</math> and <math>Fred(\mathcal H)</math>. Then the K-theory of <math>M</math> consists of the homotopy classes of sections of this bundle.

We can make this yet more complicated by introducing a trivial

:<math>PU(\mathcal H)</math>

bundle <math>P</math> over <math>M</math>, where <math>PU(\mathcal H)</math> is the [[projective unitary group|group of projective unitary operators]] on the Hilbert space <math>\mathcal H</math>. Then the group of maps

:<math>[P\rightarrow Fred(\mathcal H)]_{PU(\mathcal H)}</math>

from <math>P</math> to <math>Fred(\mathcal H)</math> which are [[equivariant]] under an action of <math>PU(\mathcal H)</math> is equivalent to the original groups of maps

:<math>[M\rightarrow Fred(\mathcal H)].</math>

This more complicated construction of ordinary K-theory is naturally generalized to the twisted case. To see this, note that <math>PU(\mathcal H)</math> bundles on <math>M</math> are classified by elements <math>H</math> of the third [[integral cohomology group]] of <math>M</math>. This is a consequence of the fact that <math>BPU(\mathcal H)</math> topologically is a representative [[Eilenberg–MacLane space]]

:<math>K(\mathbf Z,3)</math>.

The generalization is then straightforward. Rosenberg has defined

:<math>K_H(M)</math>,

the twisted K-theory of <math>M</math> with twist given by the 3-class <math>H</math>, to be the space of homotopy classes of sections of the trivial <math>Fred(\mathcal H)</math> bundle over <math>M</math> that are covariant with respect to a <math>PU(\mathcal H)</math> bundle <math>P_H</math> fibered over <math>M</math> with 3-class <math>H</math>, that is

:<math>K_H(M)=[P_H\rightarrow Fred(\mathcal H)]_{PU(\mathcal H)}.</math>

Equivalently, it is the space of homotopy classes of sections of the <math>Fred(\mathcal H)</math> bundles [[associated bundle|associated]] to a <math>PU(\mathcal H)</math> bundle with class <math>H</math>.

==Relation to K-theory==

When <math>H</math> is the trivial class, twisted K-theory is just untwisted K-theory, which is a ring. However, when <math>H</math> is nontrivial this theory is no longer a ring. It has an addition, but it is no longer closed under multiplication.

However, the direct sum of the twisted K-theories of <math>M</math> with all possible twists is a ring. In particular, the product of an element of K-theory with twist <math>H</math> with an element of K-theory with twist <math>H'</math> is an element of K-theory twisted by <math>H+H'</math>. This element can be constructed directly from the above definition by using adjoints of Fredholm operators and construct a specific 2 x 2 matrix out of them (see the reference 1, where a more natural and general Z/2-graded version is also presented). In particular twisted K-theory is a module over classical K-theory.

==Calculations<!--'K-theory (physics)' redirects here-->==

Physicist typically want to calculate twisted K-theory using the [[Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence]].<ref>A guide to such calculations in the case of twisted K-theory can be found in [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0005090 E8 Gauge Theory, and a Derivation of K-Theory from M-Theory] by [http://www.physics.rutgers.edu/people/pips/Diaconescu.html Emanuel Diaconescu], [[Greg Moore (physicist)|Gregory Moore]] and [[Edward Witten]] (DMW).</ref> The idea is that one begins with all of the even or all of the odd integral cohomology, depending on whether one wishes to calculate the twisted <math>K_0</math> or the twisted <math>K^0</math>, and then one takes the cohomology with respect to a series of differential operators.  The first operator, <math>d_3</math>, for example, is the sum of the three-class <math>H</math>, which in string theory corresponds to the Neveu-Schwarz 3-form, and the third [[Steenrod square]],<ref>(DMW) also provide a crash course in Steenrod squares for physicists.</ref> so<blockquote><math>d_3^{p,q} = Sq^3 + H</math></blockquote>No elementary form for the next operator, <math>d_5</math>, has been found, although several conjectured forms exist. Higher operators do not contribute to the <math>K</math>-theory of a 10-manifold, which is the dimension of interest in critical [[superstring theory]]. Over the rationals [[Michael Atiyah]] and [[Graeme Segal]] have shown that all of the differentials reduce to [[Massey product]]s of <math>M</math>.<ref>In [https://arxiv.org/abs/math.KT/0510674 Twisted K-theory and cohomology].</ref>

After taking the cohomology with respect to the full series of differentials one obtains twisted <math>K</math>-theory as a set, but to obtain the full group structure one in general needs to solve an [[extension problem]].

===Example: the three-sphere===
The three-sphere, <math>S^3</math>, has trivial cohomology except for <math>H^0(S^3)</math> and <math>H^3(S^3)</math> which are both isomorphic to the integers. Thus the even and odd cohomologies are both isomorphic to the integers. Because the three-sphere is of dimension three, which is less than five, the third Steenrod square is trivial on its cohomology and so the first nontrivial differential is just <math>d_3 = H</math>. The later differentials increase the degree of a cohomology class by more than three and so are again trivial; thus the twisted <math>K</math>-theory is just the cohomology of the operator <math>d_3</math> which acts on a class by cupping it with the 3-class <math>H</math>.

Imagine that <math>H</math> is the trivial class, zero. Then <math>d_3</math> is also trivial. Thus its entire domain is its kernel, and nothing is in its image. Thus <math>K^0_H(S^3)</math> is the kernel of <math>d_3</math> in the even cohomology, which is the full even cohomology, which consists of the integers.  Similarly <math>K^1_H(S^3)</math> consists of the odd cohomology quotiented by the image of <math>d_3</math>, in other words quotiented by the trivial group. This leaves the original odd cohomology, which is again the integers. In conclusion, <math>K^0</math> and <math>K^1</math> of the three-sphere with trivial twist are both isomorphic to the integers. As expected, this agrees with the untwisted <math>K</math>-theory.

Now consider the case in which <math>H</math> is nontrivial. <math>H</math> is defined to be an element of the third integral cohomology, which is isomorphic to the integers. Thus <math>H</math> corresponds to a number, which we will call <math>n</math>. <math>d_3</math> now takes an element <math>m</math> of <math>H^0</math> and yields the element <math>nm</math> of <math>H^3</math>. As <math>n</math> is not equal to zero by assumption, the only element of the kernel of <math>d_3</math> is the zero element, and so <math>K_{H=n}^0(S^3)=0</math>.  The image of <math>d_3</math> consists of all elements of the integers that are multiples of <math>n</math>. Therefore, the odd cohomology, <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>, quotiented by the image of <math>d_3</math>, <math>n\mathbb{Z}</math>, is the cyclic group of order <math>n</math>, <math>\mathbb{Z}/n</math>.  In conclusion<blockquote><math>K^1_{H=n}(S^3) = \mathbb{Z}/n</math></blockquote>In string theory this result reproduces the classification of [[D-brane]]s on the 3-sphere with <math>n</math> units of <math>H</math>-flux, which corresponds to the set of symmetric boundary conditions in the supersymmetric <math>SU(2)</math> [[WZW model]] at level <math>n-2</math>.

There is an extension of this calculation to the group manifold of [[SU(3)]].<ref>In [https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/0108100 D-Brane Instantons and K-Theory Charges] by [[Juan Maldacena]], [[Greg Moore (physicist)|Gregory Moore]] and [[Nathan Seiberg]].</ref>  In this case the Steenrod square term in <math>d_3</math>, the operator <math>d_5</math>, and the extension problem are nontrivial.
